document.title: Afghanistan: Soviet Withdrawal Scenario
document.authors: Defense Intelligence Agency, Defense Intelligence Appraisal
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: May 1988 DIA report examining plans for Soviet military withdrawal agreed between Russian diplomats and a UN negotiating team representing U.S., Pakistani, Afghan rebel and other interests.

mentions.quote: The Khalqis may also oust President Najibullah as the Soviets withdraw and then form a government that will fight the Mujahedin to the finish.

organizations.name: Mujahedin
organizations.notes: Insurgent parties expected to isolate garrisons and cities after the Soviet withdrawal; disunity among principal parties could hamper a coherent strategy.

organizations.name: People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA)
organizations.notes: Communist ruling party, split into Khalq and Parcham factions.

organizations.name: Khalq
organizations.notes: Numerous in combat units of the armed forces; supports the Geneva accords, believing it can defeat the Mujahedin without Soviet troops.

organizations.name: Parcham
organizations.notes: Dominates the government; disapproves of the withdrawal agreements.

organizations.name: Soviet Union
organizations.notes: Begins withdrawing troops from Afghanistan on 15 May 1988 under the Geneva agreements.

organizations.name: Ministry of State Security (WAD)
organizations.notes: Has combat units that are one of six components of the Afghan armed forces.

organizations.name: Ministry of Interior Sarandoi
organizations.notes: Paramilitary units of the Ministry of Interior.

organizations.name: Afghan Armed Forces
organizations.notes: Six components: army, air force/air defense, border security forces, Sarandoi, WAD combat units, and militia; high desertion.

places.name: Kabul
places.significance: Capital; last Soviet troops expected to leave by air; Mujahedin lack capability to storm it if well defended.

places.name: Northern Autonomous Zone
places.significance: Cited as a possible Communist stronghold and buffer zone against the USSR.

places.name: Geneva
places.significance: Site of the accords signed on 14 April 1988.

key_claims: The Soviet withdrawal will likely proceed by evacuating whole garrisons, with larger garrisons turned over to Afghan forces.
Mujahedin will initially focus on Afghan forces, isolating garrisons and cities, and encourage mass defections.
The Mujahedin lack the capability to storm Kabul if well defended; it may take months of pressure unless the Afghan forces collapse internally.
Khalq-Parcham rivalry could lead to factional fighting or the ousting of Najibullah.
The communist government will ultimately fall and be replaced by an uneasy coalition of traditionalist and fundamentalist groups whose control will not extend far beyond Kabul.
